statement: Whether ecstasy is followed by lower mood a few days later, the so-called mid-week low, is not settled; the evidence is insufficient to say. In a London field study (Curran and Travill, 1997), 12 people who said they had taken ecstasy at a club scored higher on the Beck Depression Inventory four days later than 12 people who had drunk alcohol (mean 11.8, SD 7.2, against 6.9, SD 4.1) and rated themselves sadder, more depressed, anxious, agitated and irritable; the paper says some were in the mild to moderate depression range but gives no count, there was no measurement before the drug night, and on the editors' calculation the day-5 difference taken alone was borderline (p = 0.053). In a Melbourne study with a baseline a week before (Scott et al., 2013), the 30 people who took ecstasy and were seen three days after use (Day 3) did not differ from the 17 seen who also use ecstasy but abstained, in distress or mood ratings; mood dropped a little in both groups, and across both groups fewer hours of sleep went with more distress and restless sleep with lower mood. The studies differ in their comparison groups (people who drank against people who use ecstasy), measures and timing, and both are small and observational. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: Some people say they feel low a few days after taking ecstasy. One small London study found that people who had taken ecstasy felt sadder mid-week than people who had only been drinking. A Melbourne study, which also measured people a week before, found no difference from people who use ecstasy but skipped it that weekend; in both groups, people who slept badly felt worse. Two small studies disagree, so nobody can yet say how often a mid-week low happens.
population: Young adults who use ecstasy, at one London club (aged 20 to 27) or recruited by advertisement in Melbourne (aged 18 to 35)
exposure: Ecstasy tablets taken at a weekend, by self-report; contents not tested (amounts are study conditions in the study cards)
comparator: People who drank alcohol but took no illicit drug that night (London, no pre-drug baseline); people who use ecstasy but abstained that weekend, against each person's own baseline (Melbourne)
outcome: Depressive symptoms, mood, anxiety, irritability and distress three to four days after use
magnitude: London, day 5: Beck Depression Inventory 11.8 (SD 7.2) against 6.9 (4.1), group x day interaction p<0.001, group main effect not significant; editors' calculation for day 5 alone: difference 4.9 points, 95% CI -0.1 to 9.9, p = 0.053, d = 0.84; depression rating 56.3 (24.4) against 20.7 (13.6) on a 100 mm scale. Melbourne, Day 3: Kessler-10 13.47 (3.68) against 12.59 (1.91) with baselines 13.43 and 14.14; mood (1-10) 5.93 (1.76) against 6.44 (1.27) with baselines 7.06 and 7.10; no group or group x time effect; K10 of 17 or more in 7 of 30 against 2 of 17 (editors' Fisher test p = 0.45).

evidence.locator: Table 2, BDI row (p. 827); Results, Beck Depression Inventory paragraph (p. 825, left column)
evidence.extracted: BDI means (SD) on days 1, 2 and 5: ecstasy group 3.5 (3.5), 8.7 (3.8), 11.8 (7.2); alcohol group 6.4 (5.3), 8.3 (5.2), 6.9 (4.1); group x day p<0.001, group not significant. The text gives the day-5 mean as 11.75, cites scores below 9 as normal and above 16 as indicating clinical depression, and says some in the ecstasy group scored in the mild to moderate range, without a count.

evidence.locator: Table 2, Sad row (p. 827); Table 3, depression, anxiety, agitation and irritability rows (p. 828); Results, Bodily Symptoms Scale paragraph (p. 826)
evidence.extracted: Day 5 ratings on visual analogue scales, ecstasy against alcohol group: sad 54.6 (27.7) against 35.1 (16.9); depression 56.3 (24.4) against 20.7 (13.6); anxiety 52.2 (21.2) against 26.9 (18.7); agitation 60.8 (21.1) against 24.5 (15.4); irritability 63.6 (17.6) against 44.1 (18.3); in the ecstasy group these rose progressively over the days while the alcohol group followed a U-shaped course.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/MDMA/Curran_1997_WeekendHighMidweekLow..pdf (published version, scanned copy; Tables 2 and 3 read on rendered page images)

evidence.locator: Introduction, last paragraph (p. 822); Method, Participants (p. 823); Results, Participants' reported drug use (p. 824); Table 2 (p. 827); Discussion, limitations paragraph (p. 829, left column)
evidence.extracted: Qualifications: no measurement before the drug night (day 1 was tested during intoxication), volunteers recruited by snowballing at one club, intake unverified, 7 of the 12 in the ecstasy group also drank, and no simple-effect test for day 5. Editors' calculation from the printed day-5 BDI means and SDs (independent t-test, 12 per group): difference 4.9, 95% CI -0.1 to 9.9, t(22) = 2.05, p = 0.053.

evidence.locator: Table 2 (p. 56); Results, Group comparisons: mood (p. 57) and Follow-up mood: clinically significant symptoms (p. 58)
evidence.extracted: Day 3 against baseline, ecstasy group (n = 30) and abstainers (n = 17): K10 13.47 (SD 3.68) and 12.59 (1.91), baselines 13.43 and 14.14; mood 5.93 (1.76) and 6.44 (1.27), baselines 7.06 and 7.10. No main effect of group or group x time interaction for K10 or mood, and none for mood after adding covariates; mood lower than baseline at Day 3 in both groups (F(1,45) = 6.52, p = 0.01). K10 of 17 or more at Day 3 in 7 (23.3%) against 2 (11.8%), not tested.

Across both groups, hours slept before Day 3 correlated with the Day 3 K10 change (r = -0.49, p = 0.001), described as fewer hours with more distress, and restless sleep with the Day 3 drop in mood (r = 0.45, p = 0.001); in the ecstasy group restless sleep correlated with the Day 3 K10 change (r = -0.59, p = 0.001). The sign of the hours correlation is hard to reconcile with the stated change-score definition (see the study card).
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/MDMA/Scott_2013_SubacuteMoodRiskFactors.pdf (published version; minus signs checked on the rendered page)

risk_of_bias.note: London: no baseline, unverified intake, unblinded assessor, differing comparison group (ROBINS-E very high). Melbourne: self-chosen exposure, groups differing in age, sex and drug use (high).

inconsistency.note: One study found a mid-week difference and the other none; the different comparison groups and baselines may explain it, but this was not tested.

indirectness.note: Real-world weekend use in the samples studied.

imprecision.note: 24 and 56 people; the London day-5 difference has an interval touching zero (editors' calculation) and the Melbourne null has no interval.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; risk of bias, inconsistency and imprecision each -1 give very low (the floor). Status mixed: two studies disagree and the reason is not established. Insufficient evidence because neither a mid-week effect nor its absence is shown with precision. A third field study with a drug-free baseline (Parrott and Lasky, 1998; card sc_parrott_1998) measured mood two and seven days after a Saturday night and should be added by the editor from its card.
